title: Augustine's City of God: Systematic Christian Demonology
description: Augustine of Hippo composed De Civitate Dei (City of God) between 413 and 426 CE, completing the most systematic early Christian account of angels, demons, and their role in human history. Augustine drew on earlier Neoplatonic frameworks but Christianized them, arguing that fallen angels — demons — were real spiritual beings capable of influencing human affairs. His treatment of the demonic established that demons operated through deception, pacts, and the misuse of human will, providing the theological architecture for later witch-trial demonology. His earlier work De Doctrina Christiana (397 CE) had already argued that any relationship with demons constituted a form of forbidden communication, the conceptual ancestor of the diabolical pact.
historiographical_note: Stuart Clark identifies Augustine's demonology as foundational to the intellectual tradition he traces in Thinking with Demons. Augustine's insistence that demons were real, that they had pacts with humans, and that divination constituted demonic communication provided the framework early modern demonologists worked within, even when arguing with each other about specifics.
source_method: Augustine, De Civitate Dei; De Doctrina Christiana; secondary scholarship on patristic theology
